subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Reading the Narrative Aloud

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the textbook to pp. 9–13 and invites students to look at the illustrations. Students predict what the story might be about based on the pictures before any reading begins.

Teacher reads the full narrative aloud expressively, pausing briefly at the moment Chinna discovers his money is missing and again when Kamala explains why returning the extra change is the right thing to do.

Students take turns reading short passages aloud in pairs, following the text in their textbooks. Teacher listens and gently corrects pronunciation of words such as 'pineapple', 'accidentally', and 'delighted'.

Class shares one word each that stood out for them from the story; teacher lists five to eight words on the board — such as 'dejected', 'honest', and 'reward' — building a shared word wall for the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the story of Chinna, a boy who chooses honesty when he is accidentally given extra change at a fruit stall, and the reading encounter here should feel relaxed and pleasurable. Read with expressive pacing, especially Kamala's explanation about how keeping the money would be stealing, since that moment is the moral pivot of the narrative. Students who find the word 'dejected' unfamiliar can be guided to its context — Chinna coming home with drooping shoulders — without stopping the read-aloud flow.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for word wall

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.14): answer four short-response questions about Chinna's feelings and actions.

homework.task_brief: Let us Think — B. (p.14): write T or F for five true-or-false statements about the story.

time_bands.activity: Teacher does a brief shared re-reading of the key scenes — Chinna spotting the bells, losing his money, and Kamala's market conversation — with students following in their textbooks on pp. 9–13.

Let us Think — A. ("answer four questions about Chinna's feelings and actions"): teacher poses each question aloud, students think for a moment, then volunteers share their answers while teacher guides the class to find supporting evidence in the text.

Class works in pairs to write their answers to all four questions in their notebooks. Teacher circulates and prompts students who are struggling to find the relevant passage in the textbook before they write.

Two or three pairs share their answers; class discusses and refines wording together, with teacher drawing attention to how Kamala's gentle comparison — reminding Chinna of his own sadness at losing money — moved him to act honestly.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard the narrative read aloud, students now work with it as a text to read closely for meaning. A common confusion is the sequence of events around the market visit — students sometimes conflate 'Kamala promising money for the bells' with 'buying the bells', since both involve money; ask them to find the two separate episodes in the text. The fourth question, about how Chinna finally bought the bells, requires tracking back through several short paragraphs, so encourage students to use their fingers to skim rather than reading from the beginning again.

periods.activity_title: True or False: Checking Close Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — B. (p.14): judge five true-or-false statements and correct each false one.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud two or three short passages from pp. 9–13 that contain the exact details tested in the true-or-false statements — including the bell-purchase scene, the fruit-stall exchange, and Kamala comforting Chinna. Students follow in their textbooks.

Let us Think — B. ("judge five true-or-false statements and correct each false one"): students work individually, writing T or F beside each statement and, for those marked F, writing a corrected version of the sentence beneath it.
Class reviews answers statement by statement; for each false statement teacher asks a student to read out the correct version they wrote, then the class locates the confirming line in the text.
Teacher leads a quick oral recap: students call out one true fact and one corrected false fact from today's work, consolidating the story's key details.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the four comprehension questions in the previous sitting, students bring familiarity with the narrative here; the true-or-false format now asks them to hold a specific detail in mind and check it precisely. The most common error is the statement about twenty rupees of extra change — the story says ten rupees — so direct students to re-read that paragraph rather than relying on memory. Requiring a written correction of false statements, rather than simply crossing them out, pushes students to use the text as a source rather than guessing.

periods.activity_title: Listen and Sequence: Retelling the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.18): listen to the story read aloud, then number six sentences in story sequence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the six sentences from the sequencing task on the board in scrambled order and reads each one aloud so students are familiar with the language before listening begins.

Let us Listen ("listen to the story read aloud, then number six sentences in story sequence"): teacher reads the full story aloud from the textbook at p. 18's indicated passage, slowly and clearly, pausing at the ends of key episodes. Students listen with pencils down.
Teacher reads the story a second time. Students now number the six sentences on the board — or in their notebooks — in the order the events occur.
Students compare their sequences with a partner. Pairs that disagree on any item go back to the text together to settle the order.
Teacher calls on volunteers to give the correct sequence one sentence at a time; the class confirms each step, building the full ordered list on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The six sentences cover the whole arc of the story — from Chinna wanting the bells to returning the extra money — so the sequencing task is effectively a listening-comprehension check on the entire narrative. Students most often swap the order of 'Chinna bought the bells after getting money from his mother' and 'Chinna went to the market with his mother', since both involve the market; encourage them to ask which had to happen first. Reading the passage twice is the recommended prep practice for listening tasks at this stage.

periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss: Chinna's Choice and Our Own Honesty

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — C. (p.14): guided discussion — why Chinna returned the money and personal honesty experiences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly retells the fruit-stall moment from the story — Chinna whispering about chocolates, Kamala's firm explanation, and Chinna running back to return the money — to bring the discussion prompt alive for students.

Let us Think — C., prompt 1 ("why Chinna decided to return the money instead of keeping it"): students discuss in pairs for two minutes, then share with the class; teacher asks probing questions such as "What did Kamala say that made Chinna change his mind?" and "How did Kamala use Chinna's own feelings to explain honesty?"

Let us Think — C., prompt 2 ("a time when you found something that didn't belong to you"): students share their own experiences in a structured go-round — teacher models with a brief personal anecdote first, then each student has an unhurried turn while classmates listen without interrupting.

Teacher draws the discussion together by asking the class to name the feeling Chinna had at the end of the story when he tied the bells on Tara's neck — contrasting it with his earlier dejection — connecting personal honesty to personal happiness.

periods.teacher_notes: Having sequenced the story events in the listening task, students now move from plot recall to personal reflection, which is the harder step. The second prompt asks students to share real experiences; model brevity and honesty yourself, and make it clear that 'I didn't find anything like that' is a perfectly acceptable response so no student feels pressured to invent a story. Students who remain silent during the go-round may be invited to describe how they think they would feel, rather than what they actually did.

periods.activity_title: What Would You Do? Ethical Situation Role-Play

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak (pp.18–19): respond orally to four ethical-dilemma situations.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the four 'What would you do?' situations from pp. 18–19 aloud, one at a time, ensuring students understand the scenario — broken pen, math-quiz cheating request, stolen notebook, shared snack.

Let us Speak ("respond orally to four ethical-dilemma situations"): students work in groups of four, each taking one situation. One student describes what they would do while the others listen and then ask one follow-up question each.

Groups briefly role-play their situation — one student acts as the main character, another plays the friend or classmate — performing the scenario in two to three spoken exchanges. Teacher circulates and prompts students to give reasons, not just actions.

Each group reports back one sentence: the situation they acted out and the choice they made. Teacher connects each choice back to Chinna's dilemma at the fruit stall, noting the common thread of doing the right thing even when it is difficult.

periods.teacher_notes: The four situations here echo the moral fabric of the story — they are all contexts where honesty or fairness costs something — so the discussion flows naturally from Chinna's example. Students sometimes give very brief responses ('I would tell the teacher') without reasoning; encourage them with 'What would you say to your friend?' or 'How would you feel if you didn't?' to deepen the talk. The snack-sharing situation often sparks the liveliest debate and can be allowed a little extra speaking time within the group work.

periods.activity_title: Value Words Word Search and Antonyms

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.15): locate ten value-related words in the word-search grid.
Let us Learn — C. (pp.17–18): circle the antonym of the highlighted word in each sentence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the ten target words — CALM, HONEST, LOVE, RESPECT, COURAGE, LOYAL, TRUTH, FAIR, KIND, PEACE — on the board and asks students to say aloud what each means in the context of the story, linking 'honest' and 'truth' to Chinna returning the money.

Let us Learn — A. ("locate ten value-related words in the word-search grid"): students open their textbooks to p. 15 and work individually to find and circle all ten words in the grid. Teacher sets a quick-check pair moment at the 12-minute mark so students who are stuck can compare grids with a neighbour.

Let us Learn — C. ("circle the antonym of the highlighted word in each sentence"): teacher reads each sentence aloud from pp. 17–18, students identify the highlighted word, then circle its opposite from the three options. Class checks each answer together, with teacher asking students to use the correct antonym in a new spoken sentence about Chinna.

Teacher draws two columns — WORD and OPPOSITE — on the board and fills in three of the four antonym pairs with student help, leaving one blank for the class to complete together. This closes the word-work by connecting antonyms to the story's own language.

periods.teacher_notes: The word-search grounds the session in the story's value vocabulary — words like 'honest', 'courage', and 'loyal' all describe qualities either demonstrated or tested in Chinna's experience. For the antonym task, students occasionally confuse 'opposite in meaning' with 'different in meaning', choosing 'Attractive' as the opposite of 'beautiful' because it sounds different; nudge them with 'If beautiful means nice-looking, what is the opposite of that?' The antonym 'Sell' for 'buy' is often the one that surprises students most, and linking it to the actual story transaction — Chacha selling the bells to Chinna — makes it stick.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (pp.16–17): fill in blanks using -er or -est comparative forms.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws three stick figures on the board labelled Chinna (tall), Charu (taller), and Jasmine (tallest), mirroring the textbook pictures on p. 16. Students read the three example sentences aloud together from p. 16 and teacher highlights the -er ending with 'than' and the -est ending for the whole group.

Teacher writes two or three additional example pairs on the board — using familiar names and objects — and students call out the correct -er or -est form before opening their textbooks. This oral pattern practice prepares students for the fill-in task.

Let us Learn — B. ("fill in blanks using -er or -est comparative forms"): students work through all five sentences in their notebooks, writing the complete word in each blank. Teacher circulates and prompts students who are uncertain to first check whether 'than' follows the blank — a reliable signal for -er — or whether the sentence refers to a whole group.
Teacher writes the five completed sentences on the board with student input and leads a rapid oral drill: each student reads one sentence aloud, emphasising the -er or -est ending clearly.

periods.teacher_notes: Degrees of comparison grammar is introduced through the story's own characters — Chinna, Charu, and Jasmine — so the grammar stays rooted in a familiar context rather than abstract rules. Students most commonly confuse when to use -er versus -est; the rule-of-thumb they find most reliable is: if the word 'than' appears, use -er; if you are talking about a whole group with no 'than', use -est. Watch for students doubling letters incorrectly — 'smartter' instead of 'smarter' — and address spelling briefly at the board check.

periods.activity_title: Sentence Framing: Words from the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (pp.19–20): frame original sentences using five words from the story.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes all five target words — smiling, mistake, honest, praise, careful — on the board and asks students to find each one in the story text on pp. 9–13, reading the original sentence aloud when found. This shows students how the words are actually used before they write.

Teacher models writing two sentences on the board — one for 'smiling' and one for 'mistake' — thinking aloud about choosing a subject, adding a meaningful verb, and making the sentence say something real rather than just using the word. Students suggest improvements to the model sentences.

Let us Write — A. ("frame original sentences using five story words"): students write one sentence each for all five words independently in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, asking students to read each sentence quietly to themselves first to check it makes sense before moving on.

Students pair up and read their sentences to each other. Each listener gives one spoken comment — what they liked or a word that could be changed — and then they swap roles. Teacher selects two or three varied sentences to read aloud to the class as closing examples.

periods.teacher_notes: The five words — smiling, mistake, honest, praise, careful — are all story-active: they appear in moments of moral significance in Chinna's experience. Students sometimes write definitions rather than sentences ('Honest means telling the truth') — gently redirect these by asking 'Who is being honest? What are they doing?' to keep sentences event-based. The peer-share at the end is brief by design; students at this stage benefit more from hearing varied sentences read aloud than from extended written revision.

periods.activity_title: Bell Craft: Making a Tinkling Bell from Recyclable Materials

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (pp.20–22): create a tinkling bell craft using recyclable materials following the step-by-step instructions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the materials list and the eleven steps of the bell-craft activity from pp. 20–22 aloud, demonstrating each step with the collected materials on the teacher's desk so students see the process before they begin.

Let us Do ("create a tinkling bell craft using recyclable materials"): students work at their desks following the steps — filling their small container with pebbles or beads, sealing or threading the string, wrapping in foil, and decorating. Teacher circulates to assist with tying knots and using the hole punch safely.

Students write a short two-sentence label for their bell in their notebooks — naming what material they used and one thing they would do differently next time — connecting the making activity to reflective writing.

Students hold up their finished bells and shake them; teacher invites two or three students to say one sentence about what Chinna felt when he heard the tinkling bells in the story, linking the craft to the narrative's final scene.

periods.teacher_notes: Students need to bring small recyclable containers (metal bottle caps, small tins) and filling material (pebbles, dried beans) — inform them one sitting in advance so the class arrives prepared. If some students forget materials, pair them with a well-supplied neighbour so nobody is idle. The foil wrapping and decorating steps are the most time-consuming, so if the craft is running slow at the 20-minute mark, students can skip the cardboard-tag step and still produce a complete bell.
materials: Small metal bottle caps or small tin cans (student-brought)

periods.activity_title: Matchstick Puzzles and Bells of India Exploration

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Fun with Matchsticks (p.23): move one matchstick to correct the equation.
Let us Explore (p.23): draw or collect pictures of different types of bells found in India.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the solved example from p. 23 on the board — the numeral equation puzzle — and talks through how moving one matchstick changes the equation from wrong to right, so students understand the logic before attempting the unsolved puzzle.

Fun with Matchsticks ("move one matchstick to correct the equation"): students work individually on the unsolved puzzle from p. 23, using pencil sketches to try different moves. Teacher circulates and asks students to explain their reasoning rather than giving the answer.
Class checks the matchstick solution together; teacher draws the before and after on the board and asks two students to explain why the solution works.

Let us Explore ("draw or collect pictures of different types of bells found in India"): students draw at least two types of bells they know or can imagine — temple bells, cowbells, school bells, church bells, cycle bells — labelling each with its name and where it is used. Teacher adds to the discussion by mentioning any regional bells students may not know.

Students share one bell drawing each in a quick show-round; teacher connects Chinna's tinkling bells for his goat Tara to the wider world of bells in India, closing the chapter's work with the story's own central image.

periods.teacher_notes: The matchstick puzzle requires spatial reasoning rather than language skill, making it a refreshing change of gear; some students will solve it quickly while others need more thinking time, so the exploration drawing task provides a natural parallel activity for early finishers. For the bells-of-India exploration, prompt students who are stuck by naming two or three bells they may have heard — a bicycle bell, a temple bell, or the school bell — to seed their drawings. The connection between Chinna's tinkling bells and the diverse bell traditions in India gives this final sitting a satisfying sense of completion for the chapter.

items.source_context: Chinna's lost money, Kamala's comfort, fruit seller's extra change, honesty rewarded with bells.
items.item_stem: Read the sentences below and write T (True) or F (False) for each one.

options.text: Chinna found the bells he wanted at Chacha's shop.
Chinna kept the extra money and used it to buy the tinkling bells.
Kamala scolded Chinna angrily when he came home feeling dejected.
The fruit seller gave Chinna ten rupees more than the correct change by mistake.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — T; 2 — F (Kamala comforted Chinna gently and promised to give him money for the bells); 3 — T; 4 — F (Chinna returned the extra money to the fruit seller after his mother reminded him how sad he had felt when he lost his own money).

items.source_lo: Student retrieves and interprets information from a narrative text using a short prose story as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Chinna's lost money, Kamala's comfort, fruit seller's extra change, honesty rewarded with bells.
items.item_stem: Kamala told Chinna that using the extra ten rupees for the bells and chocolates would be stealing. In two or three sentences, explain why Chinna agreed with her and what he did next.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Chinna agreed because his mother reminded him how sad and upset he himself had felt when his own money went missing, helping him understand how the fruit seller would feel. Moved by this, Chinna ran back to the stall and returned the ten rupees to the fruit seller.

items.source_context: Sequencing Chinna's story events; Kamala's honesty lesson; personal ethical-dilemma situations.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the story of Chinna aloud. Listen carefully. Then look at the four sentences below and number them 1 to 4 in the order they happen in the story.

options.label: A
options.text: Chinna ran back to the fruit stall and returned the extra ten rupees.

options.label: B
options.text: Chinna spotted the tinkling bells at Chacha's shop but found his money was missing.

options.label: C
options.text: Kamala took Chinna to Chacha's shop and he bought the bells.

options.label: D
options.text: The correct order is: B → Kamala comforts Chinna → Chinna and Kamala visit the market → A → C.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing only A suggests the student recalls the honesty climax but cannot place it within the full story arc.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing only B shows the student identified the story's opening problem but did not track the sequence of events that followed.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing only C suggests the student remembers the resolution but missed the events that led up to it.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are Chinna's friend and he tells you what happened at the fruit stall — that he was given ten extra rupees by mistake. Speak aloud: What would you advise him to do, and why? Give at least two reasons in your answer.

expected_elements: Advises returning the extra money to the seller.
Gives a reason rooted in fairness or honesty.
Mentions how Chinna or the seller would feel.
